transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well… I suppose the honest answer is that I got scared. I’ve been having these thoughts lately—not exactly that I’m going to do something, because I don’t have a plan to hurt myself—but thoughts like, “It would be simpler if I just didn’t wake up tomorrow.” And that’s not really like me, or at least it feels frightening to hear that in my own head.

I kept telling myself maybe it would pass, maybe I was being dramatic, but then I thought… no, if I’m thinking things like that, I probably need to talk to someone before it gets worse.
Have you been feeling down or losing interest in things you usually enjoy?

Yes… yes, I have. It’s not always dramatic, exactly. I’m not crying all day or anything like that, but most days it feels like there’s this gray film over everything. That’s the best way I can describe it. Like I’m still doing ordinary things—making a cup of tea, standing by the window, looking out at the garden—and I know, in my head, that those are things that used to feel pleasant or at least peaceful. But there’s this quiet heaviness sitting inside me, and I can’t seem to think my way out of it.

I keep trying to reason with myself, you know, telling myself, “Look, the garden is still there, the kettle is boiling, nothing terrible is happening in this moment,” but it doesn’t lift. It’s just there most days, dulling everything.
Have you noticed that even small tasks, like making the bed or getting dressed, feel more tiring than usual, or do you find yourself lacking energy even when you haven't done much?

I’m not sure, honestly. I wouldn’t want to say yes too quickly, because I don’t know that I’ve noticed a clear change in that way. I mean, at my age there are mornings when getting moving is not exactly graceful, but that’s been true for a while, and I’m not sure it’s different from usual.

With things like making the bed or getting dressed… I still do them. I may stand there a bit longer than necessary sometimes, sort of thinking my way through the next step, but I don’t know if I’d describe it as being physically tired, exactly. It’s more that I’m aware of myself doing things, if that makes sense, rather than just doing them automatically.

So… I suppose the honest answer is I haven’t really been tracking my energy closely. I can’t point to a specific “I’m exhausted even after doing nothing” kind of thing. It’s more muddled than that.
Have you noticed any changes in your ability to think clearly, concentrate, or make decisions lately?

I don’t know that I’ve noticed anything clear-cut there. I mean, I still follow conversations, and I can read the newspaper or manage ordinary decisions around the house. Sometimes I do feel a bit… slower, maybe, but then I wonder if that’s just because I’m paying too much attention to myself lately.

Decisions have never been my favorite thing if there are too many options, but I can’t honestly say there’s been some dramatic change where I can’t choose what to eat or I forget what I’m doing halfway through. I may sit with things longer than I used to, sort of turning them over in my head, but it’s hard for me to separate whether that’s concentration or just… being preoccupied.

So I suppose my answer is: not in a way I could point to confidently. Nothing that has really alarmed me like, “Oh, my mind isn’t working.” More just that everything feels a bit harder to settle on, perhaps, but I’m not sure.
Do you find that activities you used to enjoy, like hobbies or spending time with loved ones, feel less pleasurable or meaningful to you lately?

Yes… I think that’s actually one of the clearer things I’ve noticed. I used to paint a little—watercolors, mostly. Nothing terribly impressive, but I liked it. I liked laying out the little pans of color, and the brushes, and watching how the light changed things. I could spend quite a long time just trying to get the shade of a leaf or the edge of a cloud right, and that used to feel… absorbing, I suppose. Quietly satisfying.

Lately I’ll still take the things out sometimes, almost out of habit. I’ll set the paper down and put water in the jar and arrange everything as if I’m going to begin. And then I just sit there looking at the blank paper. It isn’t that I can’t physically do it, or even that I’ve decided I don’t like painting anymore. It’s more that the feeling I’m waiting for just doesn’t arrive. The color and the light are there, but they don’t seem to reach me in the same way.

After a while I usually pack it all away again, and that feels sad in a very quiet way. Like I’m going through the motions of being someone who still enjoys it, but the enjoyment itself is missing.
How long have you been feeling this way, with the gray film over everything and the heaviness most days?

It’s been… about eight months, I’d say. I’ve tried to think about when it really started, because it didn’t feel like someone flipped a switch all at once, but when I look back, it seems tied to when my brother’s health and behavior changed so suddenly.

That was around the time everything began to feel different—like the color drained out gradually, or I stopped being able to meet the day in the usual way. At first I thought, well, of course I’m upset, of course things feel off, because it was such a shock. But it hasn’t really lifted. It’s been most days since then, more or less, so yes… around eight months.
Have you found that you no longer get any pleasure out of most activities, not just the ones you used to enjoy like painting?

I’m not sure I’d say “most activities” with confidence, because I haven’t really tested everything, if that makes sense. But with painting, yes, very much so. I still sometimes go through the whole little ritual of it—I take out the watercolor box, get the brushes, put water in the jar, lay the paper down—and I’ll sit there as if something is going to start.

And then… nothing really comes. I’ll look at the blank paper, or at the colors, and I remember that I used to feel something from that—the light, the way the paint moved, even just mixing a shade. It used to give me this quiet pleasure. Now I’m sort of waiting for that feeling to arrive, and it doesn’t. After a while I just put it all away again.

So I suppose the pleasure has gone missing there, at least. It’s not that I’ve decided I dislike it. It’s more like the part of me that responded to it has gone dull.
Can you think of other activities—besides painting—that you used to enjoy, even in small ways, and whether they still feel meaningful or pleasurable to you now?

I keep coming back to the painting, I’m afraid, because that’s the clearest example for me. Other things are harder to sort out, but with the watercolors it’s so obvious because I can see the whole difference.

I’ll still set everything out sometimes—the little pans of color, the brushes, the jar of water, the paper taped down just so—and part of me thinks, “All right, maybe today I’ll feel it again.” I’ll look at the light on something, or think I might paint a leaf or the sky, and I remember how that used to pull me in. It wasn’t dramatic pleasure, not like excitement, but it had meaning for me. It made the day feel softer somehow.

Now I just sit there. I stare at the paper, and the colors are there, but they don’t seem to do anything inside me. It’s like I’m waiting for the old feeling to arrive, and it simply doesn’t. After a while I feel rather foolish sitting there with everything prepared, so I put it all away again.

So… I don’t know if I can give you a good list of other activities. But I can say that with painting, the pleasure I used to feel in color and light just doesn’t really come anymore.
Are there other things you used to enjoy—even small, everyday things—that now feel less pleasurable or meaningful to you?

I know you’re asking for other things, and I’m trying to think of a tidy answer, but the honest one is that the clearest thing is still the watercolor. It’s almost like I keep checking it, as if it might tell me whether I’m still myself.

I’ll set everything out—the paints, the brushes, the paper, the water—and I’ll sit there looking at it. I used to get this small lift just from the colors, from the light on the paper, even before I painted anything. Now I wait for that feeling to come, and it just… doesn’t. I end up staring at the blank page for a while, feeling sort of empty or foolish, and then I pack it all away again.

So yes, at least with that, something that used to feel meaningful and pleasurable mostly just doesn’t reach me now.
Can you think of any other small, everyday things—besides painting—that used to give you a sense of pleasure or meaning, even if just briefly, and whether they still feel that way to you now?

I’m sorry, I know I keep circling back to the same example, and you’re asking about other small things. I suppose I’m struggling to separate them out clearly. The watercolor is the one that tells the story most plainly, if that makes sense.

I still do the whole thing sometimes. I’ll get the paints out, set the brushes beside me, fill the little jar with water, choose a piece of paper—sometimes I even tape it down properly, as if that will make it easier to begin. And for a moment there’s almost a memory of how it used to feel. I used to love the color itself, and the way light would change what I was seeing. That could give me such a quiet sort of pleasure.

But now I just sit there looking at the paper. I wait for that feeling to arrive, and it doesn’t. The colors are there, the light is there, everything is technically the same, but it doesn’t seem to reach me. After a while I feel silly for having made all the effort, and I put it all away again.

So I can’t give you a very good list of other everyday pleasures. I can only say that this one small thing that used to mean something to me mostly doesn’t feel that way now.
Can you think of any other small, everyday things—besides painting—that used to give you a sense of pleasure or meaning, even if just briefly, and whether they still feel that way to you now?

I know you’re asking “besides painting,” and I’m not trying to be difficult, but I keep finding that my mind goes back there because it’s the clearest way I can describe what’s changed.

I still sometimes go through all the motions with the watercolors. I’ll get the paints out, fill the water jar, lay out the brushes, choose the paper—sometimes I’ll sit with it all arranged in front of me for quite a while. And I remember very clearly that there used to be pleasure in just the color and the light, even before I’d made anything. It felt quiet, but it mattered.

Now I’ll sit there staring at the blank paper, almost waiting for that old feeling to switch on. And it just doesn’t arrive. The colors are still pretty, I suppose, if I think about it logically, but they don’t seem to reach me. After a while I feel foolish for having set everything out, and I put it all away again.

So I’m sorry, I can’t seem to give you a neat list of other small pleasures. This is the one I can point to and say, yes, that used to mean something to me, and now most of the time it just doesn’t.
Can you think of any other small, everyday things—besides painting—that used to give you a sense of pleasure or meaning, even if just briefly, and whether they still feel that way to you now?

I realize I’m not answering the “other things” part very well. I’m sorry. I think the trouble is that when I try to think of small pleasures, my mind keeps landing on the watercolor because it’s the most obvious example I can actually describe.

I still do set everything out sometimes—the paints, the brushes, the paper, the little jar of water—and I almost go through it like a routine I remember. But then I’ll just sit there, staring at the blank paper. I used to feel something even before I started, just from the colors and the light, that quiet little feeling of interest or pleasure. Now I wait for it, and it doesn’t really come.

After a while I feel a bit foolish sitting there with all of it laid out, and I just put it away again. So I know you’re asking beyond painting, but that’s the one I can point to clearly: the pleasure I used to get from it just doesn’t seem to arrive anymore.
Can you think of any other small, everyday things—besides painting—that used to give you a sense of pleasure or meaning, even if just briefly, and whether they still feel that way to you now?

I know I’m still not giving you much besides the painting, and I’m sorry for that. It’s just the example that comes up most clearly for me.

I still sometimes set out my watercolor things—the paints, the brushes, the paper, the water—and I’ll sort of prepare everything as if I’m about to begin. And I remember that I used to get pleasure just from looking at the colors, or seeing the light on something and thinking how I might try to capture it. It wasn’t a big dramatic feeling, just a small, quiet one, but it was real.

Now I can sit there with everything ready, staring at the paper, and it’s like I’m waiting for that feeling to arrive. And it doesn’t. The color and light are still there, but they don’t seem to touch me in the same way. After a while I just feel a bit foolish and put everything away again. So I suppose that’s the clearest small everyday thing I can describe—the pleasure I used to feel in it just doesn’t really come anymore.
Can you think of any activity at all—no matter how small—that still brings you even a little bit of pleasure or interest these days?

I wish I could say yes easily. I’ve been trying to think of something small, because I know you’re asking “anything at all,” but the only thing that really comes to mind is still the watercolor, and even that doesn’t exactly bring pleasure now.

Sometimes I’ll still get everything out—my paints, the brushes, the paper, the water jar—and I’ll arrange it all the way I used to. There’s a kind of habit in it, I suppose, almost like I’m hoping that if I set the scene properly, the feeling will come back. I’ll sit there looking at the colors, or at the blank paper, and I remember how it used to feel when color and light would catch me a little. It didn’t have to be anything grand. Just that small spark of interest, that quiet pleasure.

But now I mostly just sit there waiting for it, and it doesn’t seem to arrive. After a while I feel a bit silly, like I’m pretending to be someone I used to be, and I put it all away again. So… no, I can’t honestly think of an activity that still gives me much pleasure. I keep trying with the one that used to, but it doesn’t reach me the way it did.
Can you think of any other activity—no matter how small—that used to bring you even a little pleasure, even before this period began?

I know you’re asking for something other than the watercolor, and I’m trying not to circle back to it again, but honestly that’s still the example my mind goes to most clearly.

Before this all began, it wasn’t even always the painting itself. Sometimes it was just setting things out—the paper, the brushes, the little pans of color, the jar of water—and noticing how the light hit something, or how a color looked when it spread on the paper. That used to give me this small, quiet pleasure, like a little moment of interest. It made me feel connected to something, I suppose.

Now I still do the same setup sometimes, almost out of habit. I’ll lay everything out and sit there looking at the blank paper, waiting for that feeling to come. But it just doesn’t, really. The colors are there, the light is there, all the same things are in front of me, but they don’t seem to reach me the way they used to. After a while I just feel a bit foolish sitting there, and I put everything away again.

So yes, before this period, that used to bring me pleasure—even the smallest parts of it did. But now it mostly feels like I’m remembering pleasure rather than actually feeling it.

Can you think of any small daily routines, interactions, or moments—like a morning cup of tea, a walk, or talking with a friend—that used to bring you even a quiet sense of comfort or pleasure, and whether they still feel that way to you now?

I’m sorry, I know you’ve asked it in a broader way—tea, walks, friends, ordinary little things—and I’m trying to think in that direction. But the honest answer is that the thing I can describe most clearly is still the watercolor.

It used to be part of the day in a very small, comforting way. Not always even making a proper painting, just setting everything out—the paper, the brushes, the little pans of color, the water. There was something gentle about that routine. I’d notice the way light fell across the table, or how one color looked next to another, and it would give me this quiet little feeling of pleasure or interest. Nothing dramatic, but it mattered.

Now I still do it sometimes. I’ll put everything out almost exactly the same way, as if following the steps might bring the feeling back. But then I just sit there staring at the blank paper. The colors are there, the light is there, but the pleasure I used to feel from it just doesn’t seem to arrive. After a while I feel sort of foolish and tired of sitting there waiting, so I put it all away again.

So I suppose it used to be a daily sort of comfort, yes. But now it feels more like I’m going through the motions of something that used to mean something to me.
Would you say that you have completely lost interest or pleasure in almost everything you used to enjoy, not just painting, but in general?

Yes… I think I would say it’s close to that, in general. I hesitate because “completely” sounds so absolute, and I keep wanting to be fair or precise about it, but the truth is that the feeling I used to get from things just isn’t there the way it was.

The watercolor is the clearest example for me, because it used to reliably give me something—just a little pleasure, a little interest. Even the colors and the light used to matter to me. And now I’ll still set everything out sometimes, almost as if I can coax that feeling back by arranging the paper and brushes and water the same way. But then I just sit there staring at the blank paper, and the pleasure doesn’t arrive. After a while I put it all away again.

So yes, not just painting exactly, but that kind of enjoyment in things generally feels like it’s gone or very hard to reach. It’s more like I remember that I used to enjoy things than actually feeling the enjoyment now.
Would you say that you have completely lost interest or pleasure in almost everything you do, not just the things you used to enjoy, but in general?

Yes… I think in general, yes, though I still stumble a bit over the word “completely.” It isn’t that I never do anything at all, or that I don’t remember what pleasure is supposed to feel like. It’s more that when I do things, the feeling doesn’t really come with them anymore.

The watercolor is still the best way I can explain it. I’ll sometimes set everything out—the paper, the brushes, the colors, the water—almost like if I arrange it all properly, some part of me will respond. I used to notice the way the colors spread or how the light looked on the table, and there was a small pleasure in that. A quiet sort of lift.

Now I can sit there staring at the paper, with everything right in front of me, and it just feels flat. The color and light are there, but they don’t seem to reach me. And after a while I just put it all away again, because I’m not really doing it, I’m just waiting for the pleasure to arrive and it doesn’t.

So… yes, in general, most things feel that way now. Like I can go through the motions, but the interest or enjoyment that used to be attached to them is missing.

I still sometimes go through the whole little ritual of it—I take out the watercolor box, get the brushes, put water in the jar, lay the paper down—and I’ll sit there as if something is going to start.

It used to give me this quiet pleasure. Now I’m sort of waiting for that feeling to arrive, and it doesn’t. After a while I just put it all away again.

So I suppose the pleasure has gone missing there, at least. It’s not that I’ve decided I dislike it. It’s more like the part of me that responded to it has gone dull.
